query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An intermediate aging treatment applied post-deformation will increase the coercive field in an AlCoFeNi-type high-entropy alloy by inducing a fine-scale phase decomposition into B2 and A2 regions that act as effective domain-wall pinning centers.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoFeNi-type high-entropy alloy in a deformed (or as-cast) state with a predominantly homogeneous B2 phase.
generation.intervention: Apply an aging treatment at 600–700 °C for approximately 10 hours following deformation.
generation.conditions: Magnetic characterization carried out at room temperature (or slightly elevated temperatures) under standard field sweep rates, ensuring a consistent measurement environment.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, hierarchically decomposed microstructure composed of finely dispersed B2 and A2 regions, forming nanoscale precipitates that serve as domain-wall pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: The intermediate-age treatment promotes phase decomposition. The resulting B2 + A2 microstructure creates numerous pinning centers that impede the motion of magnetic domain walls, thereby increasing the coercive field relative to a uniformly phased alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing the intermediate aging treatment will exhibit a significant increase in coercivity (on the order of roughly a 50% enhancement) compared to baseline samples that are as-deformed or conventionally annealed.
generation.baseline: AlCoFeNi samples that have not received the intermediate aging treatment and thus maintain a more homogeneous B2 phase.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected specifically under controlled aging conditions (600–700 °C for 10 hours); deviations in temperature or time may not produce the same degree of phase decomposition and thus may not yield the predicted coercivity enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of coercivity enhancement is subject to variability in microstructural evolution and aging homogeneity; while a significant increase is anticipated, the precise percentage change may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoFeNi-type high-entropy alloy samples with identical processing up to the deformation stage. Subject one set to the targeted intermediate aging treatment (600–700 °C for 10 hours) and leave the other set as a baseline (as-deformed or conventionally annealed). Ensure that all other processing parameters remain constant.
measurements: Measure the coercive field (Hc) of both sets using vibrating sample magnetometry under identical field-sweep conditions.
Perform microstructural analysis (e.g., via TEM or X-ray diffraction) to confirm the presence or absence of the fine-scale B2 + A2 decomposition in treated versus baseline samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercive field (for instance, less than about a 10% improvement relative to the baseline) and if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the formation of a fine-scale phase-separated structure, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The saturation magnetization (MS) and coercivity (Hc) for the four different samples analyzed in the present study have been listed in Table 1. The MS of AlCoFeNi is substantially higher compared to that of the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy for both heat-treated conditions. While the magnetization is primarily determined by composition and the crystal structure, the coercivity can be affected by impurities, deformation, grain size and phase decomposition. The coercivity (Hc) decreased with increasing annealing temperature from 15 Oe for sample aged at 600 °C/15 h, exhibiting nanoscale phase separation, to 4 Oe for samples aged at 1000 °C/15 h, exhibiting a homogeneous undecomposed B2 matrix. A similar observation has been reported in the literature, where the coercivity of the AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA annealed at 1000 °C/2 h decreases by 30 Oe (from 45 Oe to 15 Oe) compared to as-cast alloys. The AlCoFeNi HEA investigated in the present study exhibits higher saturation magnetization and lower coercivity than other soft ferrite magnetic materials, e.g., MnZn ferrite, Cu-Zn-Ti ferrite,, as revealed in Supplementary Table 2.

The microstructure and magnetic properties of AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEAs for two different annealing conditions were investigated. The focus was on probing the influence of changing the Co/Cr ratio (replacing Co by Cr) and temperature, on the phase decomposition and its consequent impact on magnetic properties and microhardness, in these HEAs. While the AlCoFeNi alloy exhibits a compositionally homogeneous single B2 phase on annealing at higher temperatures (1000 °C), it tends to decompose into a two-phase mixture of B2 + BCC on annealing at lower temperatures (600 °C). Substituting half of the Co by Cr, resulting in the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA, strongly enhances the tendency of phase separation in these alloys to form a two-phase B2 + BCC mixture for all annealing temperatures. Furthermore, annealing at 600 °C, leads to a hierarchical microstructure with multiple length scales of decomposition ranging from few nanometers to microns. This decomposition leads to a substantially higher microhardness coupled with a decrease in saturation magnetization (MS) and increase in coercivity (HC). decision.trend: In 2018, researchers (PMC6197204::webcard) showed that tuning the microstructure of AlCoFeNi-type high-entropy alloys via phase decomposition could raise coercivity (although achieved there by partial Co–Cr substitution). Later work (PMC8961229::webcard) revealed that hierarchical B2 + A2 phase separation and associated magnetic vortex states increase coercive fields in AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi. However, a proven single-step protocol, independent of additional alloying, to harness multi-phase decomposition for systematically raising coercivity remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: A consistent, non-alloying route to achieve stable and reproducible enhancements in coercivity—by deliberately introducing and controlling phase separation or precipitates—has not yet been concretely established for magnetic high-entropy alloys.
decision.lever: Apply an intermediate-temperature (e.g. 600–700 °C) aging treatment for ∼10 hours post-deformation to induce a refined B2 + A2 microstructure and enhance domain-wall pinning.
decision.why: Prior evidence (PMC6197204, PMC8961229) shows that phase decomposition and hierarchical nanostructures can raise coercivity by creating new domain-wall pinning sites. The testable hypothesis is: 'A post-deformation aging treatment at 600–700 °C for ∼10 hours will increase the coercive field in AlCoFeNi-type alloys by 50% or more, via the formation of finely dispersed B2 and A2 regions that impede domain-wall motion.' Under typical magnetic characterization conditions (room temperature or slightly elevated temperature and standard field sweep rates), samples with this aged microstructure should exhibit higher coercivity compared to as-cast or conventionally annealed references. A clear falsification would be if careful magnetic measurements (e.g., by vibrating-sample magnetometry) after this treatment reveal no significant increase in coercivity relative to the baseline.
